claims.claim: A trojan horse is malware that appears to have a useful function while carrying a hidden, potentially malicious function; it is a disguise rather than a self-spreading program.
The name 'trojan horse' comes from the wooden horse of the Trojan War in Greek mythology — a gift that looked harmless but carried hidden soldiers who opened the city from inside.
Trojans reach a device only with the user's help: they arrive bundled with downloads, inside fake installers, or hidden in email attachments, and take effect when the user runs the disguised program.

A trojan's payload varies: common ones include a backdoor giving an attacker remote access, theft of data such as passwords and browsing history, and delivery of further malware (including ransomware).
The core danger of a trojan is that it bypasses the user's trust: the user installs the disguised program willingly, and the hidden function can exploit the user's own legitimate permissions.

Signs of a trojan infection are general rather than specific: unexpected programs appearing, changed settings such as a new browser home page, slower performance, and unexpected pop-ups are clues, not proof.

Defense against trojans relies on ordinary habits: download only from official sources, check what an installer adds, think before opening attachments, and keep software updated — installing updates as soon as they are available.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Some vendor pages call trojans 'Trojan horse viruses', which can blur the line between trojans and viruses.
positions: Kaspersky's page title uses the phrase 'Trojan Horse Virus'
NIST SP 800-83 describes trojan horses as self-contained and nonreplicating, and NIST's taxonomy lists viruses, worms, and trojan horses as distinct types of malicious code
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows NIST: a trojan does not replicate and is not a virus; the 'virus' in the vendor title is a colloquial misnomer, and the lesson says so explicitly in Common Mistakes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether trojans always require user action to arrive.
positions: Kaspersky: trojans can only get onto a device with the help of the user
A few exotic surveillance trojans have reportedly been installed remotely with little or no user interaction
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the general model that NIST and Microsoft describe — trojans depend on the user installing or running the disguised program — which is the accurate picture for the awareness level; the rare remote-install exceptions are out of scope and would muddy the core teaching point.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Special Publication 800-83 Rev. 1: Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the PDF directly from nvlpubs.nist.gov on 2026-08-21. Supports: the working definition of malware as a program covertly inserted with intent to destroy data or compromise confidentiality, integrity, or availability; malware as the most common external threat to most hosts; infection routes (email attachments, malicious websites, drive-by download/web-based malware, removable media); prevention (patch management and vulnerability mitigation, antivirus software as the most common technical control, user awareness including not opening suspicious attachments even from known senders, least privilege); and the honest framing that incidents will still occur and technical controls cannot prevent all incidents. The document itself states it is not subject to copyright in the United States; used as REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: Microsoft Learn: Explain malware (Explore malware and threat protection module)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports the plain-language definition (malicious software attackers design to harm computer systems, including damage, remote access, and collecting/transmitting sensitive information) and the family one-liners: viruses replicate by inserting code into files; worms replicate without direct intervention and spread across networks without user action; trojan horses provide remote access; ransomware encrypts data and demands payment; spyware tracks use without consent.

sourceRecords.title: Microsoft Security 101: What Is Malware? Definition and Types
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21 (page updated January 13, 2025). Supports: malware definition (software designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorized access); infection routes (infected email attachments, malicious websites, unsafe downloads, infected USB drives, exploits hidden in ads on legitimate websites); signs of infection (slow performance, frequent crashes, unexpected pop-ups or programs, browser redirects, changed settings, unexpected account activity); prevention (keep software updated, antivirus solutions, backups); and the observation that attackers constantly evolve their methods.

sourceRecords.title: Update Software (Secure Our World)
sourceRecords.notes: Registered id reused from the phase-1 source registry with an identical URL. cisa.gov blocked direct fetching on 2026-08-21, so the page was read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org snapshot 2026-08-06, status 200). Supports: technology providers issue software updates to patch security weak spots and if they are not installed they cannot protect users; install updates as soon as possible; turn on automatic updates; the story of Veda shows out-of-date software and clicking an unexpected link enabling malicious activity, used for the human-error vulnerability example. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary — trojan horse
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Computer Security Resource Center
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Provides the attributed working definition: a trojan horse is a computer program that appears to have a useful function but also has a hidden and potentially malicious function that evades security mechanisms (CNSSI 4009-2015); a second definition (NIST SP 800-28) calls it a useful or seemingly useful program that contains hidden code of a malicious nature that executes when invoked. The lesson quotes the first definition briefly with attribution; facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: What is a Trojan Horse Virus? Types and How to Remove it (Kaspersky Resource Center)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Reputable vendor explainer used as a secondary source. Supports: the myth of the wooden horse of Troy as the origin of the name; trojans reach a device only with the user's help (opening attachments, downloading from unsafe sources); payload variety (banking trojans, backdoor trojans, dropper/downloader trojans that deliver further malware such as ransomware); defense checklist (obtain programs only from secure sources, think before opening attachments, keep operating system and programs updated). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
